summary.text: Orbital eccentricity is a number with no units that measures how far an orbit strays from a perfect circle.
A value of 0 is a circle, values between 0 and 1 are ellipses, exactly 1 is a parabola, and anything above 1 is a hyperbola.
Earth's orbit is nearly circular at about 0.0167, but pulls between the planets move it between about 0.0034 and 0.058 over hundreds of thousands of years.

facts.label: Word origin
facts.value: Greek ekkentros, meaning 'out of the center'

items.prompt: A comet is found with an eccentricity a little greater than 1. What does that tell you about its path?

options.label: It travels a near-perfect circle around the Sun
It follows a long ellipse and will come back
It is on a hyperbola and will leave the Solar System
It is falling in a straight line into the Sun

items.explain: Eccentricity above 1 means a hyperbola, an open path; the comet C/1980 E1, at 1.057, will eventually leave the Solar System.

items.prompt: Mercury has the most stretched orbit of any planet. How does the sunlight reaching it at its closest point compare with its farthest point?

options.label: About twice as much
Exactly the same
About 5% more
About ten times as much

items.explain: Mercury's eccentricity of 0.2056 is enough for it to get twice as much solar irradiation at perihelion as at aphelion.

items.prompt: An object's orbit has its eccentricity raised step by step from 0 toward 1. How does the shape of its path change?

options.label: It shrinks into a smaller and smaller circle
It stretches from a circle into a longer ellipse
It tilts further away from the Sun's equator
It keeps the same shape but is traced faster

items.explain: Eccentricity 0 is a circle and values between 0 and 1 are ellipses, more stretched the closer the value gets to 1.

items.prompt: Over hundreds of thousands of years, the shape of Earth's orbit drifts between rounder and more oval. What makes it change?

options.label: The Sun slowly burning away its own mass
Large asteroids striking Earth now and then
Changes in how far Earth's axis is tilted
Gravitational pulls among the planets

items.explain: Earth's orbital eccentricity varies from nearly 0.0034 to almost 0.058 as a result of gravitational attractions among the planets.

items.prompt: Most asteroids have more stretched orbits than most planets. What is the likely reason?

options.label: The Sun's magnetic field bending their paths
Jupiter's pull and collisions in the past
Their being born outside the Solar System
Sunlight pushing harder on such small bodies

items.explain: Asteroids average an eccentricity of 0.17, probably because of Jupiter's influence and past collisions.

items.prompt: Halley's Comet has an orbit with eccentricity just below 1. What does that mean for its path?

options.label: It is almost a perfect circle, like Venus's
It is a hyperbola that will carry it away
It is a very long ellipse, so it returns
It is a straight drop into the Sun

items.explain: Values between 0 and 1 are ellipses; Halley's 0.967 makes a very stretched ellipse, and comets on orbits below 1 come back.

paragraphs.heading: How far from a circle
paragraphs.text: Orbital eccentricity is a single number, with no units, that tells you how far an orbit strays from a perfect circle. A value of 0 means a circle. Anything between 0 and 1 gives an ellipse. Exactly 1 gives a parabola, the path of an object escaping or being captured, and anything above 1 gives a hyperbola.

paragraphs.heading: Earth's nearly round path
paragraphs.text: Earth's orbit has an eccentricity of about 0.0167 today, so it is close to a circle. Even so, its farthest point from the Sun, called aphelion, lies a bit farther out than its closest point, called perihelion. The far distance divided by the near one comes to about 1.03393. Over hundreds of thousands of years, the gravity of the planets pulling on each other makes Earth's value wander from nearly 0.0034 to almost 0.058.

paragraphs.heading: The planets compared
paragraphs.text: Among the planets, Mercury has the most stretched orbit, at 0.2056, with Mars next at 0.0934. That is enough for Mercury to receive twice the sunlight at its closest point that it gets at its farthest. Venus has the roundest orbit of any planet, at 0.0068, with Neptune close behind at 0.0086. Before it lost planet status in 2006, Pluto, at about 0.248, was counted as the planet with the most eccentric orbit.

paragraphs.heading: Moons and asteroids
paragraphs.text: Our Moon's value is 0.0549, the highest among the large moons of the Solar System. The four Galilean moons, Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto, all sit below 0.01. Neptune's largest moon, Triton, at just 0.000016, has the roundest orbit of any known moon, while Neptune's smaller moon Nereid reaches 0.75. Most asteroids fall between 0 and 0.35, averaging 0.17, probably because of Jupiter's pull and old collisions.

paragraphs.heading: Comets near the edge
paragraphs.text: Comets have values that differ a great deal from one to the next. Periodic comets mostly fall between 0.2 and 0.7, but some come very close to 1, such as Halley's Comet at 0.967. Comet Hale–Bopp, at 0.9951, stays just under 1, so its orbit is an ellipse and it will come back. Comet C/1980 E1, at 1.057, has the highest value of any known hyperbolic comet from our own Solar System, and it will one day leave the Solar System for good.

paragraphs.heading: Where the word comes from
paragraphs.text: The word goes back to the Greek ekkentros, meaning out of the center, by way of Medieval Latin eccentricus. Eccentric first turned up in English in 1551. An adjective form followed in 1556.
